concepts.label: Oersted's Discovery and the Magnetic Effect of Current
concepts.cardText: A compass placed near a straight copper wire in a circuit is deflected when current is passed. This means that the electric current through the wire has produced a magnetic effect, so electricity and magnetism are linked to each other. Hans Christian Oersted accidentally discovered in 1820 that a compass needle got deflected when an electric current passed through a metallic wire placed nearby, showing that electricity and magnetism were related phenomena. His research later led to technologies such as the radio, television and fibre optics.

concepts.label: Magnetic Field and Magnetic Field Lines
concepts.cardText: A compass needle is a small bar magnet whose north-seeking end is the north pole and south-seeking end is the south pole. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. The region surrounding a magnet in which its force can be detected is said to have a magnetic field. Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet line up along magnetic field lines. A magnetic field has both direction and magnitude. Its direction is the direction in which a north pole of a compass needle moves inside it, so by convention field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole outside the magnet, and run from south to north inside it: they are closed curves. Closer field lines show a stronger field, and no two field lines cross, since at a crossing the needle would have to point two ways.

concepts.topicTitle: Magnetic Field Due to a Current-Carrying Straight Conductor and the Right-Hand Thumb Rule
concepts.label: Magnetic Field Around a Straight Current-Carrying Wire
concepts.cardText: Reversing the direction of current in a wire placed over a compass reverses the deflection of the needle, so the direction of the magnetic field produced by the current is also reversed. Iron filings around a straight wire carrying current arrange in concentric circles around it: these represent the magnetic field lines, and the north pole of a compass gives their direction. When the current in the wire is increased, the deflection increases, so the magnitude of the magnetic field at a given point increases as the current increases. When the compass is moved farther from the wire with the current unchanged, the deflection decreases, so the field produced by a given current decreases as the distance from the wire increases. The concentric circles become larger and larger as we move away from the wire.

concepts.topicTitle: Magnetic Field Due to a Current-Carrying Straight Conductor and the Right-Hand Thumb Rule
concepts.label: The Right-Hand Thumb Rule
concepts.cardText: A convenient way of finding the direction of the magnetic field associated with a current-carrying conductor is the right-hand thumb rule. Imagine holding a current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand with the thumb pointing in the direction of the current. Then your fingers wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines of the magnetic field. This rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule: if we imagine driving a corkscrew in the direction of the current, the direction of rotation of the corkscrew is the direction of the magnetic field. For a current flowing east to west in a horizontal power line, the field at any point above or below turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.

concepts.topicTitle: Magnetic Field Due to a Current Through a Circular Loop and a Solenoid
concepts.label: Magnetic Field Due to a Current-Carrying Circular Loop
concepts.cardText: When a straight wire is bent into a circular loop carrying current, the concentric circles of the field around every point of the wire become larger and larger as we move away from the wire. By the time we reach the centre of the loop, the arcs of these big circles appear as straight lines. Every section of the wire contributes to the field lines in the same direction within the loop, by the right-hand rule. The field produced by a current-carrying wire at a given point depends directly on the current, so a circular coil with n turns produces a field n times as large as a single turn, because the current in each turn has the same direction and the fields of the turns add up.

concepts.topicTitle: Magnetic Field Due to a Current Through a Circular Loop and a Solenoid
concepts.label: Magnetic Field in a Solenoid and the Electromagnet
concepts.cardText: A coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely in the shape of a cylinder is a solenoid. The field pattern around a current-carrying solenoid is similar to that around a bar magnet: one end behaves as a magnetic north pole and the other as the south pole. The field lines inside the solenoid are parallel straight lines, so the magnetic field is the same at all points inside, that is, it is uniform. A strong magnetic field produced inside a solenoid can magnetise a piece of magnetic material, like soft iron, placed inside the coil. The magnet so formed is called an electromagnet.

concepts.topicTitle: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field and Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
concepts.label: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field
concepts.cardText: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that exerts a force on a magnet near it. André-Marie Ampère suggested that the magnet must also exert an equal and opposite force on the current-carrying conductor. In an aluminium rod suspended between the poles of a horse-shoe magnet, passing a current displaces the rod. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the displacement, and interchanging the magnet's poles, which reverses the field, also reverses the force. So the force on the conductor depends on the direction of the current and the direction of the field. The displacement is largest, or the force highest, when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.

concepts.topicTitle: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field and Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
concepts.label: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule and Devices Using the Force
concepts.cardText: When the current and the magnetic field are perpendicular to each other, the force is perpendicular to both. These three directions are given by Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the middle finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb points in the direction of motion or force acting on the conductor. Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include the electric motor, electric generator, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments. Remember that the direction of current is taken opposite to the motion of electrons.

concepts.topicTitle: Domestic Electric Circuits, Earthing, Overloading and Short-Circuiting
concepts.label: Domestic Circuits: Live, Neutral and Earth Wires
concepts.cardText: Homes receive electric power through the mains, by overhead poles or underground cables. One wire, usually with red insulation, is the live (positive) wire, and another with black insulation is the neutral (negative) wire. In our country the potential difference between them is 220 V. They pass into an electricity meter through a main fuse and, via the main switch, to line wires supplying separate circuits: often one of 15 A rating for high-power appliances like geysers and air coolers and another of 5 A for bulbs and fans. The earth wire, with green insulation, is connected to a metal plate deep in the earth near the house, as a safety measure for appliances with a metallic body. It provides a low-resistance path for current, so any leakage of current to the metallic body keeps its potential at that of the earth and the user does not get a severe shock. Appliances are connected in parallel so each has an equal potential difference, with its own switch.

concepts.topicTitle: Domestic Electric Circuits, Earthing, Overloading and Short-Circuiting
concepts.label: Overloading, Short-Circuiting and the Fuse
concepts.cardText: Electric fuse is an important component of all domestic circuits. A fuse prevents damage to the appliances and the circuit due to overloading. Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact, which happens when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance; the current in the circuit then abruptly increases, which is called short-circuiting. The fuse prevents damage by stopping the flow of unduly high electric current: the Joule heating in the fuse melts it and breaks the circuit. Overloading can also occur due to an accidental hike in the supply voltage, or by connecting too many appliances to a single socket.
